segments.text: Your phone is never really alone. It stays connected to a mobile tower, and that connection can catch a criminal.
A tower is a base station. Its antennas split the area around it into sectors, often three, like slices of a pizza. Your phone uses the one with the strongest signal.
Each tower sector has a Cell ID. Every call, SMS or data session notes which cell served you.
Move around, and your phone hops from tower to tower, leaving footprints.
Those footprints live in the Call Detail Record: who called whom, when, for how long, from which handset, and through which tower. Internet use is logged too, in the IPDR.
Changed the SIM? The handset has its own IMEI number, and it shows up in the records too, linking the new SIM to the same phone.
At a crime scene, police can ask for a tower dump: every phone that used the nearby towers in that window. Match two scenes, and one number stands out.
But a tower is not GPS. It shows an area, not an exact spot. Tighter in cities, much wider in villages.
Courts and police can require operators to produce these records under Section 94 of the BNSS. And operators must keep them for at least two years.
In court, a CDR needs a certificate under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam. Without it, the Supreme Court has held, it is not admissible.
And it cuts both ways. The same records can prove an innocent person was somewhere else. Save this, and share it.
